Lorentz force.explanation: Comparing $\hat{j}$ components: $-B_0 v_x = 3 \implies B_0 v_x = -3\text{ N}$.

Lorentz force.question: A charged particle of charge $q$ and mass $m$ is accelerated through a potential difference $V$ and then projected perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $B$. The angular frequency $\omega$ of revolution:
Lorentz force.explanation: Cyclotron angular frequency is $\omega = \frac{qB}{m}$, which depends only on charge $q$, mass $m$, and field $B$. It is completely independent of velocity, kinetic energy, or accelerating potential $V$.

Lorentz force.question: A uniform magnetic field $B$ is directed along the $+z$-axis. An electron enters with velocity $\vec{v} = v_0\hat{i}$. Its position vector as a function of time $t$ (with $\omega = eB/m$) is given by:
Lorentz force.explanation: At $t = 0$, $x = 0, y = 0$. $\vec{F} = -e(v_0\hat{i} \times B\hat{k}) = +e v_0 B\hat{j}$. The electron curves into $-y$ (wait: $-e(\hat{i}\times\hat{k}) = -e(-\hat{j}) = +e\hat{j}$, so initial acceleration is $+y$). Thus $v_y(t) = v_0\sin\omega t$ or similar. Integrating gives circular trajectory passing through origin.

Lorentz force.question: An alpha particle ($q = 2e, m = 4\text{ u}$) and a proton ($q = e, m = 1\text{ u}$) have the same velocity. If the alpha particle executes a circle of radius $20\text{ cm}$ in a uniform magnetic field, the radius of the proton's path in the same field is:
Lorentz force.explanation: $r = \frac{mv}{qB}$. For alpha: $r_\alpha = \frac{4}{2}\frac{v}{B} = 2\frac{v}{B} = 20\text{ cm} \implies \frac{v}{B} = 10\text{ cm}$. For proton: $r_p = \frac{1}{1}\frac{v}{B} = 10\text{ cm}$.

Lorentz force.question: A charged oil drop of mass $m$ and charge $q$ is in equilibrium between two horizontal plates in an electric field $E$. If a magnetic field $B$ is also applied horizontally, the drop will:

options.text: Begin to move in a circle

Lorentz force.explanation: Since the drop is initially stationary ($v = 0$), the magnetic force $\vec{F}_B = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B}) = 0$. The electrostatic force still balances gravity, so the drop remains completely stationary.

Lorentz force.question: A particle of mass $m$, charge $q$, and kinetic energy $K$ enters a transverse magnetic field $B$. What will be the kinetic energy of the particle after a time interval $t = 2\pi m / qB$?
Lorentz force.explanation: Magnetic force does zero work on a charged particle at every instant. The kinetic energy remains strictly constant at all times, so after any time interval it is still $K$.

Lorentz force.question: Two ions having masses in the ratio $1 : 2$ and charges in the ratio $1 : 2$ enter a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly with the same speed. The ratio of their periods of revolution is:
Lorentz force.explanation: Period $T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB} \propto \frac{m}{q}$. Ratio is $\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \frac{m_1/q_1}{m_2/q_2} = \frac{1/1}{2/2} = 1 : 1$.

Lorentz force.question: A proton is moving along the positive $z$-axis in a magnetic field $\vec{B} = B_0\hat{k}$. The magnetic force on the proton is:
Lorentz force.explanation: Since $\vec{v}$ is parallel to $\vec{B}$, the cross product $\vec{v} \times \vec{B} = (v\hat{k}) \times (B_0\hat{k}) = 0$. Hence the magnetic force is zero.

Lorentz force.question: A charged particle moves in a circle of radius $R$ in a magnetic field $B$. If the kinetic energy of the particle is doubled, the new radius of the circle will be:
Lorentz force.explanation: $r = \frac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB} \propto \sqrt{K}$. If $K' = 2K$, $r' = \sqrt{2} R$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: The force per unit length between two infinitely long, thin parallel wires separated by distance $d$ carrying currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ in vacuum is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: By Ampere's force law, the force per unit length between two parallel currents is $\frac{dF}{dL} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: Two parallel conductors carrying currents in the same direction attract each other because:

options.text: Electrostatic charges of opposite signs accumulate on them
The magnetic force between parallel currents is attractive
Electrons in one wire attract protons in the other

Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Applying the right-hand rule for magnetic field and Lorentz force shows that currents in the same direction attract each other, whereas currents in opposite directions repel.

Force between two parallel currents.question: One ampere is defined as that steady current which, when maintained in each of two infinitely long parallel conductors of negligible cross-section placed $1\text{ m}$ apart in vacuum, produces a force between them of:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Setting $I_1 = I_2 = 1\text{ A}$ and $d = 1\text{ m}$: $\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 (1)(1)}{2\pi(1)} = \frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7}}{2\pi} = 2 \times 10^{-7}\text{ N/m}$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A straight wire of length $L$ carrying a current $I$ is placed in a uniform magnetic field $B$ at an angle $\theta$ to the field. The magnitude of magnetic force on the wire is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: The magnetic force on a straight current-carrying segment in a uniform magnetic field is $\vec{F} = I(\vec{L} \times \vec{B})$, so its magnitude is $F = I L B \sin\theta$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A horizontal wire of mass $10\text{ g}$ and length $1\text{ m}$ carries a current of $2\text{ A}$. What minimum magnetic field is required to support the weight of the wire? (Take $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$)
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: For magnetic force to balance gravity: $I L B = m g \implies B = \frac{mg}{IL} = \frac{0.01 \times 9.8}{2 \times 1} = 0.049\text{ T}$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A planar current loop of area $A$ carrying current $I$ has $N$ turns. Its magnetic dipole moment $\vec{M}$ is defined as:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: The magnetic dipole moment of a planar coil is given by $\vec{M} = N I \vec{A}$, where $\vec{A}$ is the area vector perpendicular to the plane of the loop (by right-hand rule).

Force between two parallel currents.question: The torque experienced by a magnetic dipole $\vec{M}$ in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: The torque on a magnetic dipole in a uniform magnetic field is $\vec{\tau} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B}$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: The potential energy of a magnetic dipole $\vec{M}$ in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: The magnetic potential energy is defined as $U = -\vec{M} \cdot \vec{B} = -M B \cos\theta$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A magnetic dipole is in stable equilibrium in a uniform magnetic field when the angle between $\vec{M}$ and $\vec{B}$ is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: At $\theta = 0^\circ$, $U = -MB$ is a minimum and torque is zero, representing stable equilibrium. At $\theta = 180^\circ$, $U = +MB$ is a maximum, representing unstable equilibrium.

Force between two parallel currents.question: The work done in rotating a magnetic dipole of moment $M$ in a uniform magnetic field $B$ from $\theta = 0^\circ$ to $\theta = 90^\circ$ is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: $W = U(90^\circ) - U(0^\circ) = (-MB \cos 90^\circ) - (-MB \cos 0^\circ) = 0 - (-MB) = MB$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: The work done in rotating the same dipole from $\theta = 0^\circ$ to $\theta = 180^\circ$ is:
An electron moves in a circle of radius $r$ with speed $v$. The ratio of its orbital magnetic dipole moment to its orbital angular momentum (the gyromagnetic ratio) is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Magnetic moment $M = I A = \left(\frac{e v}{2\pi r}\right)(\pi r^2) = \frac{1}{2}e v r$. Angular momentum $L = m v r$. The gyromagnetic ratio is $\frac{M}{L} = \frac{e v r / 2}{m v r} = \frac{e}{2m}$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: The Bohr magneton $\mu_B$ represents the elementary quantum of magnetic moment and is defined as:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: According to Bohr's postulate, $L = n\hbar$. For $n = 1$, the orbital magnetic moment is $\mu_B = \frac{e}{2m_e}\hbar = \frac{e\hbar}{2m_e} = \frac{eh}{4\pi m_e} \approx 9.27 \times 10^{-24}\text{ A}\cdot\text{m}^2$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: Two long parallel wires separated by $20\text{ cm}$ carry currents of $5\text{ A}$ and $10\text{ A}$ in opposite directions. The force on a $2\text{ m}$ length of each wire is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: $\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d} = \frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 5 \times 10}{0.2} = 5.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N/m}$. For $L = 2\text{ m}$: $F = 5.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ N}$. Since currents are antiparallel, the force is repulsive.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A rectangular loop of sides $a = 10\text{ cm}$ (parallel to wire) and $b = 5\text{ cm}$ (perpendicular) carries current $2\text{ A}$. It is placed at distance $2\text{ cm}$ from a long wire carrying $20\text{ A}$. The net force on the loop is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Near side ($d_1 = 2\text{ cm} = 0.02\text{ m}$, attractive): $F_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2 a}{2\pi d_1} = \frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 20 \times 2 \times 0.10}{0.02} = 4.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N}$. Far side ($d_2 = 7\text{ cm} = 0.07\text{ m}$, repulsive): $F_2 = \frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 20 \times 2 \times 0.10}{0.07} = 1.14 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N}$. Net force is $F_{\text{net}} = F_1 - F_2 = (4.0 - 1.14) \times 10^{-5} = 2.86 \times 10^{-5}\text{ N}$ towards the wire.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A square loop of side $l$ carrying current $I$ is placed in a uniform magnetic field $B$. If the angle between the normal to the loop and $\vec{B}$ is $30^\circ$, the magnitude of torque experienced by the loop is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: $\tau = M B \sin\theta = (I A) B \sin 30^\circ = I l^2 B \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2} I l^2 B$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A circular loop of radius $r$ carrying current $I$ is free to rotate in a uniform magnetic field $B$. In which orientation will the loop experience maximum torque?

options.text: When the plane of the loop is parallel to the magnetic field
When the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the magnetic field
When the plane of the loop is inclined at $45^\circ$ to the field
Torque is constant for all orientations

Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Torque is $\tau = M B \sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the normal (area vector) and $\vec{B}$. Maximum torque occurs when $\theta = 90^\circ$, which corresponds to the plane of the loop being parallel to the magnetic field lines.

Force between two parallel currents.question: Three long parallel wires $A, B, C$ are equally spaced by distance $d$ in a plane. Wires $A$ and $C$ carry current $I$ into the page, and the central wire $B$ carries current $I$ out of the page. The net force per unit length on wire $B$ is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Wire $A$ exerts a repulsive force on $B$ away from $A$ (towards $C$), while wire $C$ exerts an equal repulsive force on $B$ away from $C$ (towards $A$). The two equal and opposite forces cancel out, giving zero net force on $B$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: In the previous configuration, the net force per unit length on wire $A$ is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Force from wire $B$ ($d$ away, antiparallel $\implies$ repulsive, away from $B$): $F_B = \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi d}$ (directed left). Force from wire $C$ ($2d$ away, parallel $\implies$ attractive, towards $C$, i.e., right): $F_C = \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi(2d)} = \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{4\pi d}$. Net force is $F_B - F_C = \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi d} - \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{4\pi d} = \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{4\pi d}$ directed away from $B$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A rigid wire loop carrying current $I$ has an arbitrary irregular shape in a plane, enclosing area $A$. If placed in a uniform magnetic field $B$ parallel to its plane, the torque on the loop:

options.text: Depends on the specific shape of the loop
Depends on the perimeter of the loop
Depends only on the enclosed area $A$ and equals $I A B$

Force between two parallel currents.explanation: The magnetic moment of any planar loop is $\vec{M} = I \vec{A}$, where $A$ is the enclosed area regardless of the shape. When $\vec{B}$ is in the plane of the loop, $\theta = 90^\circ$, so torque $\tau = M B = I A B$ strictly depends on area, not shape.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A wire of length $L$ carries current $I$. To maximize the magnetic dipole moment, the wire should be bent into:

options.text: A coil with multiple circular turns

Force between two parallel currents.explanation: For a given perimeter $L$, the circle encloses the maximum area ($A = L^2 / 4\pi$). Furthermore, a single turn ($N=1$) has $A_1 = L^2/4\pi$, while $N$ turns each have perimeter $L/N$ and area $A_N = (L/N)^2/4\pi$, giving total moment $M = N I A_N = I L^2 / (4\pi N)$, which is maximized when $N = 1$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: An electron of mass $m_e$ revolves around a nucleus in an orbit of radius $r$ with angular momentum $L$. The magnetic dipole moment $\vec{M}$ and angular momentum $\vec{L}$ are related vectorially by:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Because the electron carries negative charge ($-e$), the effective conventional current flows opposite to the direction of velocity. Hence the magnetic moment vector $\vec{M}$ is antiparallel to the orbital angular momentum vector $\vec{L}$: $\vec{M} = -\frac{e}{2m_e}\vec{L}$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: Two long parallel wires carrying equal currents $I$ are separated by distance $2d$. A third parallel wire carrying current $I_0$ in the same direction is placed midway between them. The net force per unit length on the third wire is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: The two outer wires are equidistant from the center wire and carry identical currents, producing equal and opposite attractive forces on the center wire. The net force is zero.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A closed current-carrying loop of any arbitrary 3D shape placed in a uniform magnetic field experiences:

options.text: Zero net torque, but non-zero net force
Non-zero net force and non-zero net torque
Zero net force and zero net torque always
Zero net force, but generally non-zero net torque

Force between two parallel currents.explanation: In any uniform magnetic field, the net force on any closed loop is $\vec{F} = \oint I (d\vec{l} \times \vec{B}) = I \left(\oint d\vec{l}\right) \times \vec{B} = 0$, because $\oint d\vec{l} = 0$. However, the net torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B}$ is generally non-zero unless aligned.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A circular coil of 50 turns and radius $7\text{ cm}$ carries a current of $4\text{ A}$. It is suspended in a uniform horizontal magnetic field of $0.5\text{ T}$. The maximum torque that can act on the coil is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Area $A = \pi r^2 = \frac{22}{7} \times (0.07)^2 = 0.0154\text{ m}^2$. Dipole moment $M = N I A = 50 \times 4 \times 0.0154 = 3.08\text{ A}\cdot\text{m}^2$. Maximum torque is $\tau_{\max} = M B = 3.08 \times 0.5 = 1.54\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: Two parallel wires carrying currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ in opposite directions are separated by distance $r$. If the current in each wire is doubled and the separation distance is halved, the force per unit length between them increases by a factor of:
A current $I$ flows in a circular loop of wire of radius $R$. The magnetic dipole moment of the loop has the dimensions of:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: $M = I A$, so $[M] = [I][A] = \text{A} \cdot \text{m}^2 = [\text{A L}^2]$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A small circular coil of radius $R$ and $N$ turns carrying current $I$ is placed in a non-uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$. The coil will experience:

options.text: Only a net torque, force is always zero
Only a net force, torque is always zero
Both a net force and a net torque in general

Force between two parallel currents.explanation: In a non-uniform magnetic field, $\vec{F} = \nabla(\vec{M} \cdot \vec{B}) \ne 0$. In general, the dipole experiences both a translational force and a rotational torque.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A coil of magnetic moment $M$ is placed with its axis along the magnetic field $B$. The work done in rotating it through $60^\circ$ is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: $W = -MB(\cos 60^\circ - \cos 0^\circ) = -MB(1/2 - 1) = \frac{1}{2}MB$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: If the magnetic field is uniform, the force on a planar closed loop carrying current $I$:

options.text: Is strictly zero regardless of shape and orientation
Is zero only if the loop is circular

Force between two parallel currents.explanation: For any closed loop in a uniform field, $\vec{F} = I \oint d\vec{l} \times \vec{B} = I (\oint d\vec{l}) \times \vec{B} = 0$, as the vector sum of elements around a closed path is zero.

Force between two parallel currents.question: Two long parallel wires carry currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ ($I_1 > I_2$) in opposite directions. The magnetic field at a point midway between them is:

options.text: $\frac{\mu_0 (I_1 + I_2)}{\pi d}$ where $d$ is the distance between the wires

Force between two parallel currents.explanation: At the midpoint, distance to each wire is $d/2$. Since currents are in opposite directions, the magnetic fields from both wires point in the same direction: $B = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi (d/2)} + \frac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi (d/2)} = \frac{\mu_0(I_1 + I_2)}{\pi d}$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A particle with charge $q$ rotates in a circle of radius $R$ at frequency $f$. Its magnetic dipole moment is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Effective current is $I = q f$. Area is $A = \pi R^2$. Magnetic moment $M = I A = q f (\pi R^2) = \pi q f R^2$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A uniform flexible wire of length $L$ carries a current $I$. When placed in a strong uniform magnetic field $B$ perpendicular to its plane, the wire naturally takes the shape of:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: The magnetic radial outward forces ($I d\vec{l} \times \vec{B}$) produce uniform tension throughout the wire, maximizing the enclosed magnetic flux and driving the flexible wire into a perfect circle.

Force between two parallel currents.question: In the circular loop formed by the flexible wire in the previous question, the tension $T$ in the wire is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Radius is $R = L / (2\pi)$. For an element subtending angle $d\theta$: $2 T \sin(d\theta/2) \approx T d\theta = I (R d\theta) B \implies T = I R B = \frac{I L B}{2\pi}$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A square loop of side $a$ carrying current $I$ has magnetic moment $M$. If the same wire is bent into a circular loop, the new magnetic moment will be:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Wire length $L = 4a$. Square area $A_s = a^2 = L^2 / 16$, so $M_s = I L^2 / 16$. Circle radius $R = L / (2\pi)$, area $A_c = \pi R^2 = L^2 / (4\pi)$, so $M_c = I L^2 / (4\pi)$. Ratio $M_c / M_s = \frac{16}{4\pi} = \frac{4}{\pi}$. Thus $M_c = \frac{4}{\pi} M$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: The magnetic field produced by a magnetic dipole of moment $M$ at distance $r$ on its equatorial line is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: For a magnetic dipole, $B_{\text{axial}} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2M}{r^3}$ along $\vec{M}$, and $B_{\text{equatorial}} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{M}{r^3}$ pointing opposite to $\vec{M}$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: The ratio of magnetic field on the axis to that on the equatorial line of a short magnetic dipole at the same distance $r$ is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: $\frac{B_{\text{axial}}}{B_{\text{equatorial}}} = \frac{2M / r^3}{M / r^3} = 2 : 1$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A current $I$ is flowing in an equilateral triangular loop of side $L$. The magnetic dipole moment of the loop is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Area of an equilateral triangle is $A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}L^2$. Magnetic moment is $M = I A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} I L^2$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: Two long parallel straight wires carry currents $I$ in the same direction. What is the magnetic force per unit length on a wire if their separation is $10\text{ cm}$ and $I = 20\text{ A}$?
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: $\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi d} = \frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times (20)^2}{0.1} = \frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 400}{0.1} = 8.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ N/m}$. Since currents are in the same direction, the force is attractive.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A circular current loop of area $A$ and moment $M$ is placed in a magnetic field $B$. The frequency of small angular oscillations of the loop about its stable equilibrium axis (rotational inertia $I_0$) is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: For small $\theta$, $\tau = -MB\theta = I_0 \alpha \implies \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \left(\frac{MB}{I_0}\right)\theta = 0$. Angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{MB}{I_0}}$, so frequency is $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{MB}{I_0}}$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A long wire is suspended horizontally by two springs. When a current is passed through it in the presence of a horizontal perpendicular magnetic field, the springs extend by an additional amount $x$. If the current is reversed, the springs:

options.text: Compress by $x$ relative to the equilibrium position under gravity

Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Reversing current reverses the direction of the magnetic force $\vec{F} = I(\vec{L}\times\vec{B})$. Since it pulled downward originally (adding to gravity), it now pushes upward with equal magnitude, compressing the springs by $x$ relative to gravity equilibrium.

Force between two parallel currents.question: Two electrons move parallel to each other with the same velocity $v$. The ratio of the magnetic force $F_m$ to the electric repulsive force $F_e$ between them is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: $F_e = \frac{1}{4\pi \varepsilon_0}\frac{e^2}{r^2}$. $F_m = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{e^2 v^2}{r^2}$. The ratio is $\frac{F_m}{F_e} = \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 v^2 = \frac{v^2}{c^2}$ since $c^2 = 1/(\mu_0 \varepsilon_0)$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A rectangular loop of sides $a$ and $b$ carries current $I$. If it is rotated about an axis passing through the centers of opposite sides of length $b$, the maximum torque is:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Area is $A = a b$. Maximum torque occurs when the normal to the loop is perpendicular to $\vec{B}$, yielding $\tau_{\max} = M B = I A B = I a b B$.

Force between two parallel currents.question: A loop carrying current $I$ is placed in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$. Which quantity is independent of the choice of reference point for calculating torque?

options.text: The total magnetic torque on the closed loop

Force between two parallel currents.explanation: Because the net force on any closed loop in a uniform magnetic field is strictly zero ($\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = 0$), the torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B}$ is a pure couple and is completely independent of the choice of origin or reference point.

Force between two parallel currents.question: Two thin long wires are held parallel at distance $d$ carrying equal currents $I$. If one wire is rotated by $90^\circ$ so that they become mutually perpendicular, the net force between them becomes:
Force between two parallel currents.explanation: By symmetry, for two mutually perpendicular straight wires carrying current, the magnetic forces on segments of one wire on opposite sides of the perpendicular intersection cancel out exactly, resulting in zero net force.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: In a moving coil galvanometer, the magnetic field is made radial by using:

options.text: Concave (cylindrical) magnetic pole pieces and a cylindrical soft iron core

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Concave pole pieces combined with a cylindrical soft iron core make the magnetic field radial everywhere in the gap, ensuring that the plane of the coil is always parallel to the field lines ($	heta = 90^\circ$), yielding a linear scale $\tau = NIAB$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: In a moving coil galvanometer, the restoring torque is provided by:

options.text: The magnetic field of the permanent magnet
The torsion in the phosphor-bronze suspension strip
Eddy currents in the coil frame

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: When the coil rotates through angle $\theta$, the phosphor-bronze suspension wire twists, developing a restoring elastic torque $\tau = C\theta$, where $C$ is the torsional constant.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: The current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer is defined as:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: At equilibrium: deflecting torque equals restoring torque: $NIAB = C\theta \implies \frac{\theta}{I} = \frac{NAB}{C}$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: The voltage sensitivity of a galvanometer having coil resistance $R_g$ is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Voltage sensitivity is deflection per unit voltage: $S_v = \frac{\theta}{V} = \frac{\theta}{I R_g} = \frac{S_i}{R_g} = \frac{NAB}{C R_g}$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: If the number of turns $N$ in a moving coil galvanometer is doubled, which of the following is correct?

options.text: Current sensitivity is doubled, but voltage sensitivity remains almost unchanged
Both current and voltage sensitivities are doubled

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Doubling $N$ doubles current sensitivity ($S_i \propto N$). However, doubling $N$ also doubles the length of the wire and hence doubles the coil resistance $R_g$. Thus $S_v = S_i / R_g = (2 S_i) / (2 R_g) = S_v$ remains unchanged.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A galvanometer of resistance $G$ is converted into an ammeter of range $0$ to $I$. If $I_g$ is the full-scale deflection current, the required shunt resistance $S$ is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: In parallel, the potential difference across the shunt equals that across the galvanometer: $(I - I_g)S = I_g G \implies S = \frac{I_g G}{I - I_g}$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A galvanometer of resistance $G$ is converted into a voltmeter of range $0$ to $V$. If $I_g$ is the full-scale deflection current, the required series resistance $R$ is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: The total resistance is $R_V = R + G$. At full scale: $V = I_g(R + G) \implies R + G = \frac{V}{I_g} \implies R = \frac{V}{I_g} - G$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: The resistance of an ideal ammeter and an ideal voltmeter are respectively:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: An ideal ammeter is connected in series and should have zero resistance so it does not alter the circuit current. An ideal voltmeter is connected in parallel and should have infinite resistance so it draws zero current.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A galvanometer has a resistance of $50\;\Omega$ and gives full-scale deflection for a current of $0.05\text{ A}$. The resistance that should be connected in parallel to convert it into an ammeter of range $0$ to $5\text{ A}$ is approximately:

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A galvanometer of resistance $100\;\Omega$ gives full-scale deflection with $1\text{ mA}$. To convert it into a voltmeter of range $0$ to $10\text{ V}$, the required series resistance is:

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: The effective resistance of an ammeter consisting of a galvanometer of resistance $G$ and shunt $S$ is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Since the galvanometer and shunt are in parallel, the equivalent resistance is $R_A = \frac{G S}{G + S}$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: Phosphor-bronze is preferred for the suspension strip in a moving coil galvanometer because it has:

options.text: Low torsional constant and high tensile strength

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Phosphor-bronze has a very small restoring couple per unit twist ($C$), giving high sensitivity, combined with high mechanical tensile strength and resistance to rusting.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: In a dead-beat galvanometer, electromagnetic damping is achieved by:

options.text: Winding the coil on a metallic (usually aluminum) frame

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: As the aluminum frame rotates in the magnetic field, eddy currents are induced in the closed metallic frame. By Lenz's law, these eddy currents produce a retarding torque that quickly brings the coil to rest without prolonged oscillation.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A galvanometer has a coil of 100 turns, area $4\text{ cm}^2$, in a magnetic field of $0.02\text{ T}$. If the restoring couple of the suspension is $10^{-8}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m/degree}$, its current sensitivity is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: $S_i = \frac{NAB}{C} = \frac{100 \times (4 \times 10^{-4}) \times 0.02}{10^{-8}} = \frac{8 \times 10^{-4}}{10^{-8}} = 8 \times 10^4\text{ degrees/A}$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A galvanometer gives full-scale deflection with current $I_g$. If a shunt of value $S = G/9$ is connected across it, the new current range of the ammeter is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: $S = \frac{I_g G}{I - I_g} \implies \frac{G}{9} = \frac{I_g G}{I - I_g} \implies I - I_g = 9 I_g \implies I = 10 I_g$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: What fraction of the total circuit current passes through the galvanometer in the previous problem?
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Fraction passing through the galvanometer is $\frac{I_g}{I} = \frac{I_g}{10 I_g} = \frac{1}{10} = 10\%$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: To increase the current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer by $50\%$, the number of turns is increased. What happens to its voltage sensitivity if the resistance of the coil also increases by $50\%$?
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: $S_v = \frac{S_i}{R_g}$. When $S_i' = 1.5 S_i$ and $R_g' = 1.5 R_g$, $S_v' = \frac{1.5 S_i}{1.5 R_g} = S_v$. Voltage sensitivity remains completely unchanged.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A voltmeter of resistance $R_V$ is connected across a resistor $R$ in a circuit. The percentage error in the measured voltage is minimized when:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: When a voltmeter is placed across $R$, the equivalent resistance becomes $R_{\text{eq}} = \frac{R R_V}{R + R_V} = R\left(1 - \frac{R}{R + R_V}\right)$. To minimize loading error ($R_{\text{eq}} \approx R$), we require $R_V \gg R$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: An ammeter of resistance $R_A$ is connected in series with a resistor $R$. The percentage error in measuring current is minimized when:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Total circuit resistance becomes $R + R_A$. Current is $I' = \frac{V}{R + R_A}$. For $I' \approx I = V/R$, we require $R_A \ll R$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A moving coil galvanometer has 50 divisions. A current of $4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ A}$ gives a deflection of 10 divisions. The figure of merit of the galvanometer is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Figure of merit $k$ is the current required for unit deflection: $k = \frac{I}{\theta} = \frac{4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ A}}{10\text{ divisions}} = 4.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ A/division}$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: The full-scale deflection current $I_g$ for the galvanometer in the previous problem is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: $I_g = k \times \theta_{\text{total}} = (4.0 \times 10^{-5}\text{ A/div}) \times 50\text{ div} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A} = 2\text{ mA}$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A galvanometer has resistance $G$. A shunt $S$ is connected across it to convert it into an ammeter of range $n I_g$. The value of $S$ is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: $S = \frac{I_g G}{I - I_g} = \frac{I_g G}{n I_g - I_g} = \frac{G}{n - 1}$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A galvanometer of resistance $G$ is converted into a voltmeter of range $n V_g$, where $V_g = I_g G$. The required series resistance $R$ is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: $R = \frac{V}{I_g} - G = \frac{n V_g}{I_g} - G = \frac{n(I_g G)}{I_g} - G = nG - G = (n - 1)G$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A galvanometer of resistance $25\;\Omega$ is shunted by a $2.5\;\Omega$ wire. The part of total current that flows through the shunt is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Current through shunt is $I_s = I \frac{G}{G + S} = I \frac{25}{25 + 2.5} = I \frac{25}{27.5} = I \frac{10}{11}$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: The soft iron core in a galvanometer serves two primary functions:

options.text: Increases the magnetic field strength and makes the field radial
Provides restoring torque and reduces friction
Prevents eddy currents and cools the coil
Acts as an electrical conductor for the signal

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Because of its high magnetic permeability ($\mu_r \gg 1$), soft iron concentrates the magnetic lines of force (increasing $B$) and directs them normal to the cylindrical surface, ensuring a strictly radial magnetic field.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: Two galvanometers $A$ and $B$ have coils with details: $N_A = 30, A_A = 3.6 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2, B_A = 0.25\text{ T}, R_A = 10\;\Omega$ and $N_B = 42, A_B = 1.8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2, B_B = 0.50\text{ T}, R_B = 14\;\Omega$. If torsional constants are identical, the ratio of their current sensitivities $S_{iA} / S_{iB}$ is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: $S_i = \frac{NAB}{C}$. $\frac{S_{iA}}{S_{iB}} = \frac{N_A A_A B_A}{N_B A_B B_B} = \frac{30 \times 3.6 \times 0.25}{42 \times 1.8 \times 0.50} = \frac{27}{37.8} = \frac{5}{7}$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: For the same two galvanometers in the previous question, the ratio of their voltage sensitivities $S_{vA} / S_{vB}$ is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: $\frac{S_{vA}}{S_{vB}} = \frac{S_{iA}}{S_{iB}} \times \frac{R_B}{R_A} = \frac{5}{7} \times \frac{14}{10} = \frac{5}{7} \times \frac{7}{5} = 1$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A milliammeter of range $10\text{ mA}$ has a resistance of $1\;\Omega$. How will you convert it into a voltmeter reading up to $10\text{ V}$?

options.text: Connect a resistance of $999\;\Omega$ in parallel
Connect a resistance of $1000\;\Omega$ in series
Connect a resistance of $0.001\;\Omega$ in parallel
Connect a resistance of $999\;\Omega$ in series

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: $R = \frac{V}{I_g} - G = \frac{10}{10 \times 10^{-3}} - 1 = 1000 - 1 = 999\;\Omega$ in series.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: How will you convert the same milliammeter ($10\text{ mA}, 1\;\Omega$) into an ammeter reading up to $1\text{ A}$?

options.text: Connect a shunt of $\frac{1}{99}\;\Omega$ in parallel
Connect a shunt of $99\;\Omega$ in parallel
Connect a resistance of $99\;\Omega$ in series
Connect a shunt of $0.01\;\Omega$ in parallel

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: $S = \frac{I_g G}{I - I_g} = \frac{0.010 \times 1}{1.0 - 0.010} = \frac{0.010}{0.99} = \frac{1}{99}\;\Omega$ in parallel.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A voltmeter has a range $0$ to $V$ with resistance $R$. If its range is to be extended to $n V$, the additional resistance to be connected in series is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: At full scale, current is $I_g = V/R$. For new range $V' = nV$: total resistance $R' = \frac{nV}{I_g} = nR$. Additional series resistance is $\Delta R = R' - R = nR - R = (n - 1)R$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: An ammeter has a range $0$ to $I$ and resistance $R_A$. To extend its range to $n I$, the required shunt resistance to be connected across it is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Treating the ammeter as a meter with internal resistance $R_A$ and full-scale current $I$: $S = \frac{I R_A}{nI - I} = \frac{R_A}{n - 1}$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A galvanometer has resistance $G$. When a shunt of $4\;\Omega$ is connected across it, the deflection is reduced to $1/5$ of its initial value. The value of $G$ is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Deflection is reduced to $1/5 \implies I_g = I/5$. By shunt formula: $S = \frac{I_g G}{I - I_g} = \frac{(I/5)G}{4I/5} = \frac{G}{4} \implies 4\;\Omega = \frac{G}{4} \implies G = 16\;\Omega$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A circuit consists of a battery of EMF $6\text{ V}$ and internal resistance $1\;\Omega$ connected to a resistor of $5\;\Omega$. An ammeter of resistance $0.5\;\Omega$ is inserted to measure the current. The percentage error in the measurement is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: True current without ammeter: $I = \frac{6}{5 + 1} = 1.0\text{ A}$. Measured current with ammeter: $I' = \frac{6}{5 + 1 + 0.5} = \frac{6}{6.5} \approx 0.923\text{ A}$. Percentage error $= \frac{1.0 - 0.923}{1.0} \times 100\% = 7.7\%$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A multi-range voltmeter uses a single galvanometer with several series resistors. This combination is known as a:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: A high resistance connected in series with a galvanometer to convert it into a voltmeter is called a multiplier.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: Which of the following modifications will DEFINITIVELY increase both the current sensitivity and voltage sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer simultaneously?

options.text: Increasing the magnetic field $B$ by using stronger magnets
Using a wire of higher electrical resistivity

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Increasing $B$ increases both $S_i = \frac{NAB}{C}$ and $S_v = \frac{NAB}{C R_g}$ without changing the resistance $R_g$ or wire length.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: Why is a tangent galvanometer oriented such that its coil lies in the magnetic meridian?

options.text: To protect the needle from gravity
To cancel out Earth's vertical field component
So that the magnetic field produced at the center is perpendicular to the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: In a tangent galvanometer, the coil is placed in the magnetic meridian so that its magnetic field $B$ is perpendicular to Earth's horizontal component $B_H$. Under two perpendicular fields, the needle deflects by angle $\theta$ satisfying the tangent law $B = B_H \tan\theta$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A tangent galvanometer has 50 turns of radius $8\text{ cm}$. If the deflection of the compass needle is $45^\circ$ when placed in Earth's field $B_H = 3.9 \times 10^{-5}\text{ T}$, the current in the coil is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: By tangent law: $B = B_H \tan 45^\circ = B_H$. Field at center: $B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R} = B_H \implies I = \frac{2 R B_H}{\mu_0 N} = \frac{2 \times 0.08 \times 3.9 \times 10^{-5}}{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 50} = \frac{6.24 \times 10^{-6}}{6.28 \times 10^{-5}} \approx 0.1\text{ A}$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: In a ballistic galvanometer, the first deflection (throw) $\theta$ of the coil is directly proportional to:

options.text: The total electric charge $q$ that passed through the coil
The rate of change of current

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: In a ballistic galvanometer, a brief current pulse passes through before the coil starts moving noticeably. The initial angular impulse produces an initial angular velocity proportional to total charge $q = \int i dt$, resulting in a first throw $\theta \propto q$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A galvanometer with a resistance of $12\;\Omega$ gives a full-scale deflection for a current of $2.5\text{ mA}$. How can it be converted into an ammeter of range $0$ to $7.5\text{ A}$?

options.text: By connecting a resistance of $3000\;\Omega$ in series
By connecting a shunt of $0.04\;\Omega$ in parallel
By connecting a shunt of $0.004\;\Omega$ in parallel
By connecting a resistance of $0.004\;\Omega$ in series

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: $S = \frac{I_g G}{I - I_g} = \frac{0.0025 \times 12}{7.5 - 0.0025} \approx \frac{0.030}{7.4975} \approx 0.004\;\Omega$ in parallel.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A voltmeter of resistance $2000\;\Omega$ reads $2.0\text{ V}$ per division. The total number of divisions is 50. The current required for full scale deflection is:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Full-scale voltage is $V = 50 \times 2.0 = 100\text{ V}$. Full scale current is $I_g = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{100\text{ V}}{2000\;\Omega} = 0.05\text{ A} = 50\text{ mA}$.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: A galvanometer coil has resistance $15\;\Omega$ and the meter shows full scale deflection for a current of $4\text{ mA}$. To convert the meter into a voltmeter of range 0 to $18\text{ V}$, the required series resistor is:

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: An ammeter reads up to $1\text{ A}$. Its internal resistance is $0.81\;\Omega$. To increase the range to $10\text{ A}$, the required shunt resistance is:

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: If an ammeter is accidentally connected in parallel across a voltage source, what is the most likely consequence?

options.text: It will read the correct EMF
The pointer will not deflect at all
A very large current will pass through it, potentially burning the coil
It will act as an ideal voltmeter

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Because an ammeter has very low internal resistance ($R_A \approx 0$), connecting it in parallel across a potential difference will draw an enormous short-circuit current ($I = V/R_A$), damaging or burning out the meter.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: If a voltmeter is accidentally connected in series with a load in a circuit, what will happen?

options.text: The load will operate at double power
Almost no current will flow in the circuit, and the voltmeter will read nearly the full supply voltage

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Because a voltmeter has a very high internal resistance ($R_V \gg R$), connecting it in series reduces the circuit current to near zero. Almost the entire source voltage drops across the voltmeter, so it safely reads nearly the supply voltage.

Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.subTopic: Moving coil galvanometer and conversion to ammeter/voltmeter
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.question: The angle of deflection $\theta$ in a moving coil galvanometer with a radial magnetic field is directly proportional to:
Moving coil galvanometer and conversion.explanation: Because of the radial magnetic field, $\tau = NIAB = C\theta$, so $\theta = \left(\frac{NAB}{C}\right)I$, which is strictly linear and directly proportional to current $I$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: The relation connecting magnetic flux density $\vec{B}$, magnetic field intensity $\vec{H}$, and magnetization $\vec{M}$ in SI units is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: In SI units, the constitutive relation is $\vec{B} = \mu_0(\vec{H} + \vec{M})$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: Magnetic susceptibility $\chi_m$ of a magnetic substance is defined as:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Magnetic susceptibility is the ratio of magnetization $M$ induced in the material to the applied magnetic intensity $H$: $\chi_m = \frac{M}{H}$ (dimensionless).

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: The relative magnetic permeability $\mu_r$ of a substance is related to its magnetic susceptibility $\chi_m$ by:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: $B = \mu H = \mu_0(H + M) = \mu_0 H(1 + M/H) = \mu_0 H(1 + \chi_m)$. Hence $\mu = \mu_0(1 + \chi_m) \implies \mu_r = \frac{\mu}{\mu_0} = 1 + \chi_m$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: For a diamagnetic substance, the magnetic susceptibility $\chi_m$ is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Diamagnetic materials develop magnetization opposite to the applied field. Their susceptibility is negative, small (order of $10^{-5}$), and $\mu_r < 1$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: For a paramagnetic substance, the magnetic susceptibility $\chi_m$ is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Paramagnetic substances develop weak magnetization in the direction of the applied field, so $\chi_m$ is small and positive (order $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-3}$), with $\mu_r > 1$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: For a ferromagnetic substance, the magnetic susceptibility $\chi_m$ is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Ferromagnetic substances have domains that align strongly with the external field, producing very large magnetization, so $\chi_m \gg 1$ (often $10^3$ to $10^5$) and $\mu_r \gg 1$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: Superconductors exhibit perfect diamagnetism (the Meissner effect). For a superconductor, the magnetic susceptibility $\chi_m$ and relative permeability $\mu_r$ are respectively:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Inside a superconductor, magnetic field is completely expelled ($B = 0$). From $B = \mu_0(H + M) = 0 \implies M = -H \implies \chi_m = M/H = -1$. Then $\mu_r = 1 + \chi_m = 1 + (-1) = 0$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: Curie's law for paramagnetic substances states that the magnetic susceptibility varies with absolute temperature $T$ as:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Curie's law states that for paramagnetic substances, thermal agitation opposes dipole alignment: $\chi_m = \frac{C}{T}$, where $C$ is the Curie constant.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: Above the Curie temperature $T_c$, a ferromagnetic substance transforms into a:

options.text: Paramagnetic substance obeying the Curie-Weiss law

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Above the Curie temperature $T_c$, thermal energy destroys the spontaneous domain alignment. The substance becomes paramagnetic and obeys the Curie-Weiss law: $\chi_m = \frac{C}{T - T_c}$ for $T > T_c$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: The magnetic susceptibility of a diamagnetic substance depends on absolute temperature $T$ as:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Diamagnetism arises from the induced orbital motion of paired electrons (Lenz's law at atomic level) and is completely independent of thermal agitation and temperature.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: When a diamagnetic liquid is placed in a watch glass resting on the pole pieces of a magnet placed close together (strongest field at center), the liquid:

options.text: Accumulates at the middle, forming a mound
Accumulates at the sides, forming a depression in the middle

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Diamagnetic materials are repelled from regions of stronger magnetic field to regions of weaker magnetic field. Since the field is strongest at the center when poles are close, the liquid moves away from the center toward the sides.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: When a paramagnetic liquid is placed in the same watch glass with poles close together, the liquid:

options.text: Accumulates in the middle, forming a mound

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Paramagnetic substances are attracted toward regions of stronger magnetic field. When the poles are close together, the field is strongest in the middle, so the liquid concentrates in the middle.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: A thin rod of diamagnetic material is suspended freely in a uniform horizontal magnetic field. In equilibrium, the rod aligns itself:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: A diamagnetic rod experiences repulsion from the magnetic field lines. To minimize its interaction energy, it sets its longest dimension perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic field.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: A thin rod of paramagnetic material suspended freely in a uniform horizontal magnetic field aligns itself:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Paramagnetic materials are attracted by the magnetic field, so the rod sets its longest axis parallel to the magnetic field lines to maximize flux through it.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: In the hysteresis curve ($B$-$H$ loop) of a ferromagnetic material, the value of $B$ remaining in the material when the magnetizing field $H$ is reduced to zero is called:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Retentivity (or remanence) is the residual magnetic flux density remaining in the ferromagnetic material when the external magnetizing field $H$ is reduced to zero.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: The reverse magnetizing field $H_c$ required to completely demagnetize the ferromagnetic material (reduce $B$ to zero) is called:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Coercivity is the magnitude of the reverse magnetic intensity $H$ needed to wipe out the residual magnetism ($B = 0$).

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: The area enclosed by the $B$-$H$ hysteresis loop represents:

options.text: The energy dissipated as heat per unit volume of the material per cycle of magnetization

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: The area of the hysteresis loop equals $\oint H dB$, which represents the hysteresis energy loss per unit volume per magnetization cycle, dissipated as heat.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: For making permanent magnets, the material should have:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Permanent magnets require high retentivity (to retain a strong magnetic field) and high coercivity (so that stray magnetic fields or mechanical shocks do not demagnetize it), like Alnico or carbon steel.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: For making transformer cores and electromagnets, soft iron is preferred over steel because soft iron has:

options.text: High permeability and low hysteresis loss (narrow hysteresis loop)

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Soft iron has high magnetic permeability (easily magnetized), high saturation magnetization, and low coercivity resulting in a narrow hysteresis loop, which minimizes energy dissipation during rapid AC cycles.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: The horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field at a place is $B_H$ and the angle of dip is $\delta$. The total magnetic field $B$ of the Earth at that place is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Since $B_H = B \cos\delta$, the total field is $B = \frac{B_H}{\cos\delta}$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: At the magnetic equator of the Earth, the angle of dip (inclination) $\delta$ is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: At the magnetic equator, the magnetic field lines are strictly horizontal, so the vertical component $B_V = 0$, giving $\tan\delta = B_V/B_H = 0 \implies \delta = 0^\circ$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: At the magnetic poles of the Earth, the angle of dip $\delta$ is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: At the magnetic poles, the Earth's field lines are strictly vertical ($B_H = 0$), so a dip needle points vertically, giving $\delta = 90^\circ$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: At a place on Earth, the horizontal and vertical components of magnetic field are equal. The angle of dip at that place is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: $\tan\delta = \frac{B_V}{B_H}$. When $B_V = B_H$, $\tan\delta = 1 \implies \delta = 45^\circ$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: The angle between the magnetic meridian and the geographic meridian at a place is called:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Magnetic declination (or variation) is the angle between the geographic meridian (true north-south) and the magnetic meridian (magnetic north-south) at a given location on Earth's surface.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: A dip circle is oriented in a plane making an angle $\theta$ with the magnetic meridian. The apparent dip $\delta'$ is related to the true dip $\delta$ by:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: In a plane inclined at $\theta$ to the magnetic meridian, the vertical component is unchanged ($B_V' = B_V$), but the horizontal component is $B_H' = B_H\cos\theta$. Thus $\tan\delta' = \frac{B_V'}{B_H'} = \frac{B_V}{B_H\cos\theta} = \frac{\tan\delta}{\cos\theta}$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: If $\delta_1$ and $\delta_2$ are the apparent dips observed in two mutually perpendicular vertical planes, the true dip $\delta$ satisfies:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Let the two planes be at angles $\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$ to the magnetic meridian. $\tan\delta_1 = \frac{\tan\delta}{\cos\theta} \implies \cos\theta = \frac{\tan\delta}{\tan\delta_1} = \tan\delta\cot\delta_1$. Similarly $\sin\theta = \tan\delta\cot\delta_2$. Since $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$: $\tan^2\delta(\cot^2\delta_1 + \cot^2\delta_2) = 1 \implies \cot^2\delta = \cot^2\delta_1 + \cot^2\delta_2$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: A sample of paramagnetic salt contains $2.0 \times 10^{24}$ atomic dipoles each of dipole moment $1.5 \times 10^{-23}\text{ J/T}$. The sample is placed under a magnetic field of $0.64\text{ T}$ and cooled to a temperature of $4.2\text{ K}$. The degree of magnetic saturation achieved is $15\%$. What is the total dipole moment of the sample?
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Total maximum possible dipole moment is $M_{\max} = N m = (2.0 \times 10^{24}) \times (1.5 \times 10^{-23}) = 30\text{ J/T}$. At $15\%$ saturation: $M = 0.15 \times 30 = 4.5\text{ J/T}$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: A magnetic needle free to rotate in a vertical plane orientation at the magnetic poles will stand:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: At the magnetic poles, the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field is zero ($B_H = 0$) and the total field is purely vertical. Hence the dip needle points vertically.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: A compass needle which is allowed to move in a horizontal plane only at the magnetic poles will:

options.text: Stay in any direction (no restoring torque)

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Since $B_H = 0$ at the magnetic poles, there is zero horizontal magnetic field to exert torque in the horizontal plane. The needle experiences zero restoring couple and will rest in any arbitrary direction.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: An example of a diamagnetic substance is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Bismuth, copper, water, lead, nitrogen, and gold are classic diamagnetic substances with fully paired electron shells.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: An example of a paramagnetic substance is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Aluminum, liquid oxygen, chromium, manganese, and sodium are paramagnetic substances possessing unpaired electron spins.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: The SI unit of magnetization $\vec{M}$ and magnetic intensity $\vec{H}$ is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Magnetization is magnetic moment per unit volume ($[M] = \text{A}\cdot\text{m}^2 / \text{m}^3 = \text{A/m}$). Magnetic intensity $H$ also has units of $\text{A/m}$ (or ampere-turns per meter).

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: The magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnetic material at $-73^\circ\text{C}$ ($200\text{ K}$) is $0.0075$. Its value at $-173^\circ\text{C}$ ($100\text{ K}$) is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: By Curie's law, $\chi_1 T_1 = \chi_2 T_2 \implies \chi_2 = \chi_1 \frac{T_1}{T_2} = 0.0075 \times \frac{200}{100} = 0.0150$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: A solenoid of 1000 turns per meter has an iron core of relative permeability $\mu_r = 500$. If a current of $0.5\text{ A}$ passes through the solenoid, the magnetization $M$ of the core is approximately:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: $H = n I = 1000 \times 0.5 = 500\text{ A/m}$. Susceptibility $\chi = \mu_r - 1 = 500 - 1 = 499$. Magnetization $M = \chi H = 499 \times 500 \approx 2.5 \times 10^5\text{ A/m}$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: The primary origin of diamagnetism in atoms is:

options.text: Alignment of permanent electron spin dipole moments
Induced orbital motion of electrons according to Lenz's law

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: When an external magnetic field is applied, the orbital motion of electrons is modified such that the induced magnetic moments oppose the external field in accordance with Lenz's law. This occurs in all atoms.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: Paramagnetism occurs in atoms or molecules that have:

options.text: Zero orbital angular momentum and zero spin
Permanent magnetic dipole moments due to unpaired electrons

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Paramagnetism arises in materials whose atoms possess permanent net magnetic dipole moments from unpaired electron spins or orbital angular momenta.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: Magnetic shielding (screening a sensitive instrument from stray external magnetic fields) is accomplished by enclosing the instrument inside a container made of:

options.text: Soft iron or mu-metal (high permeability material)

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: High permeability materials like soft iron or mu-metal provide an easy, low-reluctance path for magnetic field lines, channeling them through the container walls and leaving the interior cavity virtually field-free.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: A bar magnet of magnetic moment $M$ is cut into two equal halves along its length (longitudinally). The magnetic moment of each half is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Cutting along the length halves the pole strength ($m' = m/2$) while keeping the length $2l$ unchanged: $M' = m'(2l) = (m/2)(2l) = M/2$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: If the same bar magnet of moment $M$ is cut into two equal halves transverse to its length (perpendicularly), the magnetic moment of each half is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Cutting perpendicular to the length keeps pole strength $m$ unchanged but halves the magnetic length ($l' = l$): $M' = m l = M/2$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: A bar magnet has pole strength $m$ and length $2l$. It is bent into a semicircle. The new magnetic dipole moment is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Initial moment is $M = m(2l)$. When bent into a semicircle of radius $R$: $\pi R = 2l \implies R = 2l / \pi$. The new distance between poles is the diameter $2R = \frac{4l}{\pi}$. New moment is $M' = m(2R) = m\left(\frac{4l}{\pi}\right) = \frac{2(2ml)}{\pi} = \frac{2M}{\pi}$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: A magnetic needle suspended horizontally in Earth's field oscillates with frequency $2\text{ Hz}$ at a place where $B_H = 0.4\text{ G}$. At another place where $B_H = 0.1\text{ G}$, its frequency of oscillation will be:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Oscillation frequency is $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{M B_H}{I}} \propto \sqrt{B_H}$. $\frac{f_2}{f_1} = \sqrt{\frac{B_{H2}}{B_{H1}}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.1}{0.4}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2} \implies f_2 = \frac{2\text{ Hz}}{2} = 1\text{ Hz}$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: The time period of oscillation of a magnet in a vibration magnetometer is $T$. If another identical magnet is placed symmetrically over it with like poles together, the new time period is:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Moment of inertia doubles ($I' = 2I$), and magnetic moment doubles ($M' = 2M$). Time period $T' = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I'}{M' B_H}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2I}{2M B_H}} = T$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: If the two identical magnets in the previous problem are placed with opposite poles together, the new time period of oscillation will be:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: Net magnetic moment becomes $M' = M - M = 0$. Since there is no restoring torque, the angular frequency $\omega = 0$ and the time period becomes $T' = \infty$.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: Gauss's law for magnetism states that $\oint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{A} = 0$. This fundamental law implies that:

options.text: Magnetic field lines have beginnings and ends
Magnetic force is always zero on neutral atoms
Isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: The vanishing of total magnetic flux through any closed surface means magnetic field lines form continuous closed loops with no sources or sinks, proving that isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist in nature.

Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.question: Electromagnets are made of soft iron because soft iron has:
Magnetic properties (dia, para, ferromag.explanation: An electromagnet must produce a strong magnetic field when current is on (requiring high permeability) and lose virtually all magnetism when current is switched off (requiring low retentivity and low coercivity).
